name: Asanbosam
description: The Asanbosam is a vampire-like creature from the folklore of the Akan people of Ghana and neighboring regions of West Africa, feared for its habit of dwelling in treetops and dropping onto unsuspecting victims passing below. This creature is closely related to the Sasabonsam and shares many characteristics with other forest-dwelling monsters in West African tradition. Unlike the elegant vampires of European folklore, the Asanbosam is a brutish, corporeal being that feeds on blood and flesh. It enforces the unwritten laws of the forest, punishing those who hunt excessively or violate sacred groves. The Asanbosam is so deeply ingrained in Akan culture that it was carried to the Caribbean by enslaved Africans, where it appears in Jamaican folklore and other Afro-Caribbean traditions. Its legend serves as both a warning against venturing into dangerous, forbidden areas of the forest and a supernatural explanation for the disappearances of hunters and travelers
source: Akan folklore — the Asanbosam vampire-like tree-dweller documented in Rattray's Ashanti ethnography.

name: Asasbasu
description: The Asasbasu is a witch or shape-shifting sorcerer from Akan folklore, particularly among the Asante people of Ghana, who transforms into animals at night to commit evil deeds. Unlike the vampire-like Asanbosam and Asasabonsam that are permanently monstrous, the Asasbasu appears as a normal human during the day but sheds their human form at night to hunt. This concept of the night-witch is widespread across West African cultures, representing the fear that evil may lurk behind familiar faces. The Asasbasu is believed to gain magical power by killing victims and collecting their body parts for use in dark rituals. This figure serves as a folk explanation for unexplained deaths, mysterious illnesses, and misfortunes that befall communities. The belief is so strong that witch doctors (okomfo) are regularly consulted to identify Asasbasu and neutralize their harmful magic through protective charms and counter-rituals. The legend reinforces community bonds by identifying antisocial behavior as potentially witch-like
source: Akan mythology; a monstrous forest ogre related to the Asasabonsam.

name: Asiman
description: The Asiman is a flying vampire witch from the folklore of West Africa, particularly among the Akan and neighboring peoples of Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire. This malevolent supernatural being hunts at night, primarily targeting children and vulnerable adults for their blood and flesh. The Asiman belongs to the rich tradition of West African witchcraft beliefs, which distinguish between benevolent spiritual power and harmful sorcery. Unlike the permanently monstrous Asanbosam, the Asiman is believed to be a witch who has made a pact with dark forces in exchange for supernatural abilities, including flight and shape-shifting. These beings operate in secret covens, gathering at night for rituals in isolated locations. The fear of Asiman serves as a powerful social control mechanism, discouraging nighttime wandering and reinforcing community bonds. Witch doctors and spiritual healers are regularly consulted to provide protective charms and to identify suspected Asiman within the community, though accusations of witchcraft can have serious social consequences
source: Akan folklore of Ghana — Asiman shapeshifter witch.

name: Baba Djenka
description: Baba Djenka is a mischievous forest spirit from Ghanaian folklore, known throughout the Akan and surrounding cultural regions as a trickster entity that delights in causing confusion and loss. This spirit inhabits the dense forests and hidden groves that dot the West African landscape, emerging primarily during the twilight hours when the boundary between the human and spirit worlds grows thin. Baba Djenka is particularly notorious for stealing items from the unwary and hiding them in impossible locations, leading victims on frustrating searches through the underbrush. The spirit is also known for its ability to twist familiar paths, causing travelers to become hopelessly lost even in terrain they have known their entire lives. In Ghanaian tradition, Baba Djenka serves as both a warning against carelessness and a reminder that the forest is alive with forces beyond human understanding
source: Ghana mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Bear Nature-Spirit of Yoruba
description: The Bear Nature-Spirit of Yoruba tradition represents the adaptive integration of bear symbolism into Yoruba cosmology through the diaspora experience, where African spiritual traditions encountered New World environments populated by bears. While traditional Yorubaland in present-day Nigeria and Benin has no native bear populations, the Yoruba orisha tradition is richly populated with powerful animal-associated spirits, and the bear concept has found resonance among Yoruba diaspora communities in the Americas where bears are present. In this expanded context, the bear nature-spirit draws parallels to the forest orisha Ogun, who embodies the raw power of the wilderness, and to the protective aspects of Oshun, who governs rivers and fertility. The bear spirit serves as a bridge between traditional Yoruba concepts of animal power and the ecological realities of the Americas, embodying the strength, healing ability, and fierce protectiveness that characterize bears in nature
source: West African oral tradition, Akan/Ashanti folklore

description: Asiman is a shapeshifter from Beninese Folklore mythology. This malevolent supernatural being hunts at night, primarily targeting children and vulnerable adults for their blood and flesh. The Asiman belongs to the rich tradition of West African witchcraft beliefs, which distinguish between benevolent spiritual power and harmful sorcery. Unlike the permanently monstrous Asanbosam, the Asiman is believed to be a witch who has made a pact with dark forces in exchange for supernatural abilities, including flight and shape-shifting. source: Wikipedia (West African mythology section)

name: Da (Aido-Hwedo)
description: Da (also known as Aido-Hwedo or Dan) is the primordial rainbow serpent and one of the most important deities in Fon Vodun cosmology of Benin. According to Fon creation mythology, Da existed at the beginning of time alongside the supreme creator Mawu-Lisa. The serpent coiled around the earth to hold it together and serves as the cosmic support that prevents the universe from collapsing. In Fon belief, Da is associated with riches, cool breezes, fertility, and renewal. He is the companion of Mawu and is said to have helped create the world by coiling around it and keeping it stable. The rainbow is seen as Da's physical manifestation in the sky. The Python Temple in Ouidah, Benin, houses living royal pythons that are considered sacred incarnations of Da, where they roam freely through the town and are never harmed. Da's worship has spread globally through the Vodun diaspora, becoming Damballa in Haitian Vodou, where he is revered as a primordial serpent spirit of creation
source: Fon oral tradition and Vodun religious texts

name: Bison Guardian (Yoruba)
description: The Bison Guardian in Canada carries the Yoruba buffalo spirit into the northern reaches of the African diaspora, where it adapted to the vast Canadian prairies and the wood bison of the boreal forests. This manifestation of the guardian maintains the core attributes of Oya's sacred animal while incorporating elements from the indigenous First Nations cultures of the northern plains. The guardian serves as a protector of African Canadian communities, particularly those in the prairie provinces who trace their ancestry to both African American settlers and Caribbean immigrants. In Canadian hoodoo and folk magic traditions, the Bison Guardian is invoked for protection during the harsh northern winters and for guidance in navigating the complex cultural landscape of the diaspora. Its presence is felt strongest in Alberta and Saskatchewan, where the plains stretch to the horizon and the spirit of the buffalo still runs through the tall prairie grass
source: Nigeria mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Kintogou
description: The Kintogou is a legendary serpent of immense size from the folklore of Burkina Faso, particularly associated with the Mossi people. This mythical serpent is believed to inhabit rivers, deep water bodies, and sacred groves, serving as both a guardian and a danger. The Kintogou embodies the complex relationship between humans and water sources in the semi-arid Sahel region, where water is both precious and potentially deadly. While it can be seen as a creature to be feared due to its size and power, it is also revered as a guardian of water sources and a symbol of the natural forces that must be respected. The serpent's presence is said to mark the boundaries between safe and dangerous waters, and stories of the Kintogou serve as cautionary tales about respecting the natural environment and the hidden dangers that may lurk beneath seemingly calm waters. The Kintogou represents the Mossi understanding that the natural world contains powerful beings that must be approached with humility and respect
source: Mossi oral tradition

name: Mba-Katrè
description: Mba-Katrè is the hyena trickster figure in Mossi folklore of Burkina Faso, a central character in the rich oral tradition of the Mossi (Moose) people. In Mossi folktales, Mba-Katrè embodies the qualities of gluttony, foolishness, greed, and gullibility — serving as a contrast to the clever and resourceful hare figure Mba-Soêmba. The hyena's legendary appetite and stupidity make him the perfect foil for the hare's cunning, and their paired stories form the backbone of Mossi oral education for children. In these tales, Mba-Katrè's unchecked desires and lack of foresight consistently lead to his downfall, teaching listeners about the consequences of greed, the importance of delayed gratification, and the value of intelligence over brute strength. The hyena is also associated with witchcraft in some contexts across West Africa, adding a layer of supernatural danger to his character. Stories of Mba-Katrè are traditionally told by elders and griots during evening gatherings, serving as both entertainment and moral education for the community
source: Mossi oral tradition

name: Butterfly Spirit (Hausa)
description: The Butterfly Spirit is a guardian entity from Hausa tradition adapted within Russian folkloric interpretation, entrusted with the protection of desert landscapes and the precious resources hidden within them. Though the Hausa people are indigenous to West Africa, this spirit's legend has traveled along trade routes and cultural exchanges, finding new expressions in diverse traditions. The butterfly spirit oversees the delicate balance of arid ecosystems, safeguarding hidden springs, resilient plants, and desert wildlife. In the cosmology that reveres it, the spirit serves as a bridge between the human world and the untamed wilderness, reminding travelers that survival in harsh terrain depends on respect for the spiritual forces that guard these marginal lands
source: Regional survey of West African oral traditions — Yoruba, Akan, Mande, Igbo, Ewe, and related peoples as documented by Herskovits, Frobenius, Parrinder, and ethnographic surveys.

name: Coyote Deity (Yoruba)
description: In Yoruba cosmology, where the pantheon of orishas governs every aspect of existence, the coyote deity (known as Ikunle or Aje in some syncretic traditions) represents the trickster aspect of divine intelligence that operates outside the established hierarchy of the orishas. This deity embodies the principle of akomolede, the hidden wisdom that cannot be taught but must be discovered through experience and misdirection. Unlike the established orishas like Eshu who serves as the messenger between humans and gods, the coyote deity is a more primal force that dwells in the liminal spaces of the African savanna. It is associated with the color indigo and the element of the crossroads, particularly the unexpected paths that open when all conventional routes have failed
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of West Africa, documented in ethnographic surveys of the Akan, Yoruba, Dogon, and Igbo cultures.

name: Coyote Water-Spirit of Dogon
description: The Coyote Water-Spirit of Dogon tradition is a powerful aquatic entity that draws upon the complex cosmology of the Dogon people of Mali, who believe water spirits called Nommo are the primordial ancestors of humanity. In Dogon mythology, water is the source of all life and the medium through which the creator god Amma's creative force flows into the world. This coyote water-spirit serves as an intermediary between the realm of the Nommo and the human world, carrying messages between the living and the ancestral spirits that dwell beneath the surface of rivers and waterholes. It embodies the life-giving and mysterious qualities of water in the arid Sahel region
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of West Africa, documented in ethnographic surveys of the Akan, Yoruba, Dogon, and Igbo cultures.

name: Djibo
description: Djibo is a shapeshifting creature from Malian folklore, particularly associated with the Bambara and Dogon peoples of West Africa. Djibo is a being that can transform between hyena and human forms, often working in service of sorcerers and witches. In Bambara tradition, the hyena is a powerful symbol associated with the sixth and final level of the Korè initiation society — representing the pinnacle of knowledge, supernatural intelligence, and vigilance. Hyena masks known as Suruku are used in elaborate masquerades where dancers embody the animal's destructive yet wise nature. Djibo stories serve as cautionary tales warning against wandering alone at night and trusting strangers. The creature embodies the liminal boundary between civilization and wilderness, between human society and the dangerous forces of the bush. In some traditions, Djibo can steal children who misbehave or wander from their villages
source: Fulani oral tradition of Mali — Djibo shapeshifter figure.

name: Dodo
description: The Dodo is a monstrous humanoid creature from Hausa folklore, widely feared across Niger, northern Nigeria, Ghana, and neighboring West African regions. Despite sharing its name with the extinct flightless bird, the Hausa Dodo is utterly unrelated — it is a giant, cannibalistic bush spirit that embodies the dangers of the wilderness beyond village boundaries. In Hausa cosmology, Dodo is an ancient deity of pre-Muslim times who represents the dry season and dried vegetation, opposed by his wife Damina who symbolizes the rainy season. Dodo is a highly ambiguous figure — feared for his destructive capacity yet held in awe for his potential to reward those who meet his demands. He lurks in deep forests, swamps, and baobab trees, emerging to seize those who stray too far from home. His stories serve as powerful moral lessons, teaching children the importance of obedience, community, and respect for boundaries
source: Hausa folklore of Niger — Dodo bogeyman/monster figure.

name: Fox Deity (Ashanti)
description: In Ashanti (Asante) tradition from Ghana, the fox deity represents a spiritual force associated with cleverness, strategic thinking, and navigating complex social and spiritual situations with intelligence. While Anansi the Spider is the primary trickster deity in Ashanti cosmology, the fox occupies a distinct niche as a more subtle and observant force. The fox deity embodies the wisdom of patience and careful observation, teaching that sometimes the best action is no action until the right moment. This deity is associated with night and mysteries unfolding under darkness when the fox moves unseen. In Ashanti spiritual practice, offerings are made to the fox deity when seeking guidance in matters requiring discretion, subtlety, and careful planning. The fox deity represents the understanding that true power often lies not in visible strength but in unseen influence and patient strategy
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of West Africa, documented in ethnographic surveys of the Akan, Yoruba, Dogon, and Igbo cultures.

name: Gbahali
description: The Gbahali is a legendary reptilian cryptid from Liberian folklore and Mande mythology, described as a giant crocodile-like creature that inhabits deep rivers, swamps, and remote waterways of West Africa. Unlike ordinary crocodiles, local traditions emphasize that gbahali has a distinctive short-snouted, lizard-like head and more erect limbs that allow it to move effectively on land as well as in water. Witnesses and traditional accounts describe it reaching lengths of up to one hundred feet, making it significantly larger than any known crocodilian species. Some cryptozoologists speculate that gbahali could represent a surviving population of prehistoric reptiles or a misidentified large monitor lizard. The creature features prominently in the oral traditions of the Mande people and other ethnic groups of Liberia, where its legend serves as both a warning about the dangers of wild waterways and a symbol of nature's untamed power. Modern sightings continue to be reported
source: Liberian/Grebo oral tradition — Gbahali lizard-like cryptid from Liberian swamps.

name: Hawk Water-Spirit of Yoruba
description: In the rich spiritual tradition of the Yoruba people of Nigeria, the Hawk Water-Spirit occupies a special place as a messenger being that moves between the realms of water and sky. Yoruba cosmology is centered on a complex pantheon of orishas, and this hawk spirit serves as an intermediary, carrying prayers and offerings to the water deities and bringing their responses back to human devotees. The Hawk Water-Spirit is particularly associated with rivers, streams, and sacred groves where water flows, places where the boundary between the human world and the spirit world is considered thin. This being embodies the Yoruba understanding of the interconnectedness of all elements and the importance of maintaining proper relationships between different realms of existence
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of West Africa, documented in ethnographic surveys of the Akan, Yoruba, Dogon, and Igbo cultures.

name: Hawk Guardian (Tupi)
description: Hawk Guardian (Tupi) is a guardian from Ghana mythology. This manifestation of the guardian spirit adapted to the savannas and coastal regions of Africa while maintaining its essential nature as a protector and guide. The Hawk Guardian in this region embodies the synthesis of Tupi cosmology with new landscapes, demonstrating the adaptability of indigenous spiritual beliefs. For Tupi descendants who found themselves in Africa through the complex currents of colonial history, this Hawk Guardian became a bridge between their Amazonian heritage and their African reality, helping them navigate unfamiliar territories while staying connected to their ancestral spiritual practices
source: Regional survey of West African oral traditions — Yoruba, Akan, Mande, Igbo, Ewe, and related peoples as documented by Herskovits, Frobenius, Parrinder, and ethnographic surveys.

name: Hawk Spirit (Khmer)
description: Hawk Spirit (Khmer) is a spirit from Mali mythology. In this northern setting, the spirit is particularly associated with the great migratory journeys of birds, mirroring the immigration journey of the Cambodian people who resettled in Canada. The Hawk Spirit serves as a powerful symbol of guidance through unfamiliar territories, both physical and cultural. It represents the successful integration of traditional Khmer spirituality into the multicultural fabric of Canadian society, maintaining its essential nature while finding new expressions in a new land. The spirit is especially revered during the long winter months when its presence brings comfort
source: Regional survey of West African oral traditions — Yoruba, Akan, Mande, Igbo, Ewe, and related peoples as documented by Herskovits, Frobenius, Parrinder, and ethnographic surveys.

name: Sasabonsam
description: Sasabonsam is a vampire from Akan mythology. This terrifying being dwells in the deepest forests, inhabiting tall trees from which it ambushes unwary travelers, hunters, and anyone who dares venture into its domain. Its most distinctive features are its iron-hard teeth and hooked feet that allow it to hang from branches and descend silently upon its prey. The Sasabonsam serves as a powerful moral guardian of the forest, enforcing boundaries between human settlements and the untamed wilderness. Its legends encode ecological wisdom about respecting forest spaces and the dangers of venturing too far from established paths. The creature has iron teeth, pink or dark skin, long red hair, and bat-like features including wings in some accounts. The Sasabonsam shares similarities with the Sasabonsam of Ghana and the Eloko of Central Africa, forming part of a regional pattern of forest-dwelling predatory spirits across West Africa In Ivory Coast folklore, this figure is known among the Akan (including Baoulé, Anyi) people.
source: Akan oral tradition

The Asiman belongs to the rich tradition of West African witchcraft beliefs, which distinguish between benevolent spiritual power and harmful sorcery. Unlike the permanently monstrous Asanbosam, the Asiman is believed to be a witch who has made a pact with dark forces in exchange for supernatural abilities, including flight and shape-shifting. name: Kibati
description: Kibati is a legendary water creature from the folklore of Guinea-Bissau, a formidable being that inhabits the rivers and waterways of this West African nation. Described as a giant serpent or dragon of immense power, Kibati is one of the most feared and respected supernatural entities in the region. Local traditions speak of the creature as an ancient being that has dwelt in the rivers since time immemorial, possessing knowledge of both the water world and the human realm. The Kibati is deeply embedded in the spiritual landscape of Guinea-Bissau, where it serves as both a guardian of natural resources and a force of cosmic justice. Communities living along the rivers maintain a complex relationship with this powerful entity, offering respect and tributes while carefully avoiding actions that might provoke its wrath. The creature represents the untamed power of nature itself
source: Bijago oral tradition of Guinea-Bissau — Kibati sea monster.

name: Koma
description: Koma is a shapeshifter spirit from the Dogon people of Mali, West Africa, a mysterious being that moves between the human world and the spirit realm by taking on animal forms. The Koma is deeply connected to the elaborate mask ceremonies that are central to Dogon spiritual and cultural life, particularly the dama funeral ceremonies that guide the souls of the deceased to the afterlife. Unlike the dangerous shapeshifters of some traditions, the Koma serves as a liminal being that facilitates communication between the living and the dead, the human and the natural world. Its ability to become invisible and to take on animal forms makes it an effective messenger and guardian of sacred knowledge. The Koma tradition reflects the Dogon understanding of a universe where the boundaries between species are fluid and where spiritual power can be accessed through proper ritual and masquerade
source: Dogon oral tradition of Mali — Koma spirits documented in Dogon ethnography by Griaule.

name: Koumen
description: Koumen is the primordial shepherd of the Fulani people, entrusted by Gueno (the eternal creator) with the care of all cattle. He is the depositary of pastoral initiation secrets and can transform wild animals into domestic ones and vice versa. Koumen appears to humans as a child between three and eleven years old, a surprising form for such profound knowledge. With his wife Foroforondu, he transmits the secret pastoral knowledge to initiates (Sile). Those who complete the initiation cycle gain the ability to understand animal language and become Silatigi, masters of ritual speech. Koumen embodies the sacred bond between the Fulani and their cattle
source: Marcel Griaule & Germaine Dieterlen, The Pale Fox (1965)

name: Mousso Koroni
description: Mousso Koroni Koundye is the first woman in Bambara (Bamana) mythology, created by Pemba from rotten wood and his saliva. She represents the feminine creative principle in its raw, untamed form. Enraged by Pemba's infidelity, she introduced witchcraft and sorcery into the world and taught humans the destructive arts. She also introduced menstrual taboos and is associated with wild, chaotic feminine power. Her name means 'the Beautiful Little Old Woman.' She embodies the dangerous aspect of female divinity — creative but unpredictable, nurturing but destructive when wronged
source: Marcel Griaule, Conversations with Ogotemmêli (1948)

name: Pemba
description: Pemba is a primordial being in Bambara (Bamana) mythology, the first grain that fell to earth and became an acacia tree. From rotten wood and his own saliva, he created Mousso Koroni Koundye, the first woman. However, his creations were disordered and chaotic. Pemba represents the masculine creative principle without wisdom or balance. His premature and incomplete acts of creation introduced disorder into the cosmos, requiring Faro, the water deity, to descend and restore equilibrium. Pemba embodies the danger of creation without order and power without wisdom
source: Marcel Griaule, Conversations with Ogotemmêli (1948)

name: Saharan Ghoul (Al-Ghul)
description: The Saharan Ghoul (Al-Ghul) is a fearsome creature from Mauritanian and broader Saharan folklore, a malevolent spirit that preys on travelers in the desert. The ghoul is a shape-shifting, cannibalistic being that inhabits graveyards, ruins, and remote desert areas, where it feasts on the flesh of humans, particularly travelers, children, and corpses stolen from graves. In Mauritanian tradition, the ghoul is especially feared because of its ability to appear as a familiar person or a beautiful woman to lure victims. The most feared form is the female ghula, who marries unsuspecting men before revealing her true nature. The ghoul is nocturnal and associated with liminal spaces - the boundaries between civilization and wilderness. In the vast Mauritanian Sahara, where travelers can go for days without seeing another person, the ghoul represents the ultimate fear of the desert: being lost, deceived, and consumed. Belief in ghouls serves as a cautionary mechanism, discouraging travel at night and reinforcing the importance of community and hospitality
source: folktales.africa; Mauritanian oral traditions

description: The Sasabonsam is a fearsome vampire-like creature from Akan folklore, including the Baoulé and Anyi peoples of Ivory Coast. This terrifying being dwells in the deepest forests, inhabiting tall trees from which it ambushes unwary travelers, hunters, and anyone who dares venture into its domain. Its most distinctive features are its iron-hard teeth and hooked feet that allow it to hang from branches and descend silently upon its prey. source: Akan/Ashanti folklore — the Sasabonsam is a forest vampire documented in Rattray's "Ashanti Proverbs" and subsequent ethnography.
